title: Tracking Global Compulsory Licensing Trends in Biopharmaceuticals
gist: CSIS argues that two decades of evidence show compulsory licensing almost never converts legal authority into actual drug supply — from Brazil's HIV threats and Thailand 2006-08 to the H5N1 Tamiflu episode and Covid-era CLs — because the binding constraints are manufacturing capacity, technology transfer and regulatory capability, not patent access. Meanwhile voluntary licensing (Gilead's remdesivir and Sovaldi deals, Merck's Medicines Patent Pool molnupiravir licenses) delivered measurable uptake, even as the EU, South Africa, Turkey and Latin American states now codify CL regimes as preparedness signaling.

insights.claim: Voluntary licenses in biopharma typically bundle patent rights with technology transfer, manufacturing know-how, quality assurance, regulatory support and ongoing technical assistance, whereas compulsory licensing delivers only the first step — legal access to the patent.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The right way to price CL headline risk for a patent holder: the licensable asset is the know-how bundle, not the patent, so CL destroys less economic value than headlines imply.
insights.quote: compulsory licensing is largely limited to the first step: legal access to the patent
insights.locator: The contrast is instructive.

insights.claim: Compulsory licensing is grounded in Article 31 of the WTO's 1994 TRIPS agreement, which still obliges remuneration to patent holders, and was reaffirmed as a member right by the 2001 Doha Declaration.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The legal path is well established and not going away — so the investable question is implementation capacity, not legality.
insights.locator: Compulsory licensing refers to a government authorization

insights.claim: Voluntary licensing arrangements come under stress specifically from public health emergencies, demand surges beyond manufacturing capacity, political pressure, geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption and disputes over commercial terms — a listable set of triggers for IP-override risk.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A concrete checklist for anticipating when pharma IP is politically vulnerable, useful for timing exposure to patent-dependent revenue streams.
insights.locator: However, VL arrangements can come under stress

themes.theme: Pre-Covid Track Record of CL Threats

insights.claim: Brazil's repeated threats in the early 2000s to issue compulsory licenses on HIV antiretrovirals produced some short-term price reductions but failed to build local manufacturing capability or reduce long-term import dependence.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: CL threats work as a pricing lever, not a supply lever — the realistic downside for a patent holder is margin compression, not volume loss.
insights.locator: Pre-Covid Experience with CLs

insights.claim: Thailand's use of compulsory licensing between 2006 and 2008 generated uncertainty among other countries and drew scrutiny from trading partners concerned about regulatory predictability.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Issuing a CL carries trade-relations and investment-signaling costs, which is part of why so few countries follow through.
insights.locator: Thailand’s use of compulsory licensing between 2006 and 2008

insights.claim: In the 2005 H5N1 avian influenza crisis, no country that threatened a compulsory license on Roche's Tamiflu succeeded in producing or securing additional supply, because the manufacturing process required specialized facilities and precursor materials local producers lacked; supply only expanded after Roche voluntarily sub-licensed qualified producers in China and India.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The cleanest natural experiment in the piece: process complexity, not patent law, sets the supply ceiling — argues against pricing in CL-driven volume loss for complex molecules.
insights.quote: Hence, the legal authority to override patents does little when the industrial and scientific capacity to manufacture is absent.
insights.locator: The H5N1 avian influenza crisis of 2005

insights.claim: Before the pandemic, compulsory licenses were used mainly as a bargaining tool to pressure patent holders during pricing disputes, and in most cases yielded limited or temporary results without expanding domestic production or innovation capacity.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Reframes CL announcements as negotiating theater — a reason to discount headline risk on first announcement.
insights.locator: Pre-Covid Experience with CLs

themes.theme: Covid-Era Evidence: CL Failure, VL Delivery

insights.claim: Israel was the first mover in March 2020, issuing a compulsory license to import generic lopinavir/ritonavir, while Hungary and Russia both adopted new rules and issued CLs for remdesivir and Brazil, Canada, Chile, Ecuador and Germany streamlined legal pathways — yet few of these achieved meaningful production outcomes.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A named list of jurisdictions willing to override patents under stress, and evidence that willingness did not translate into supply.
insights.locator: Between 2020 and 2022, several governments invoked

insights.claim: Gilead Sciences' 2020 voluntary licensing agreements with seven Indian manufacturers for remdesivir, plus India's Vaccine Maitri initiative supplying over 298 million Covid-19 vaccine doses to nearly 100 countries, are cited as achieving what compulsory measures could not.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Voluntary licensing to Indian generic capacity is the proven scaling channel — relevant to any thesis on Indian CDMO/generic manufacturing as a strategic asset.
insights.locator: However, the pandemic also highlighted how voluntary licensing frameworks

insights.claim: Merck's 2021 voluntary licensing deals through the Medicines Patent Pool allowed 27 generic manufacturers in India and 10 other low- and middle-income countries to produce molnupiravir.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The Medicines Patent Pool is the institutional intermediary that makes voluntary scaling politically defensible — watch it as the preferred channel in the next health emergency.
insights.locator: Further, Merck signed voluntary licensing deals

insights.claim: India and South Africa co-led the push for a TRIPS waiver at the World Trade Organization during Covid, revealing a durable split between Western innovator nations and much of the developing world over IP interpretation.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: This North-South IP fault line is the structural driver of future CL codification waves and a persistent policy risk for patent-heavy sectors.
insights.locator: Further, countries such as India and South Africa

insights.claim: Gilead's nonexclusive voluntary licenses from 2014 for hepatitis C direct-acting antivirals, including to Ferozsons Laboratories, paired patents with technology transfer and local manufacturing, and a 2019 difference-in-differences analysis found covered countries had significantly higher hepatitis C treatment uptake than comparable countries without such agreements.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The strongest quantitative evidence in the piece that VL raises access — the empirical basis for arguing voluntary tiered licensing is both commercially and politically superior to CL.
insights.locator: The rollout of direct-acting antivirals for hepatitis C

themes.theme: CL Demand Is Crisis-Driven, Not Structural

insights.claim: Calls for compulsory licenses over the past 25 years track health crises rather than any secular trend: a first rise in 2003-2005 with HIV/AIDS and SARS, a second wave in the early 2010s concentrated in Latin America (Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador) targeting HIV, cancer and hepatitis C, and the largest surge during Covid in 2020-2022.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: CL risk is episodic and event-driven — it should be priced as a tail risk correlated with pandemic onset, not a rising secular cost of doing business.
insights.locator: As Figure 1 shows, calls for CLs over the past 25 years

insights.claim: As pandemic urgency has faded, momentum for issuing new compulsory licenses has slowed even as efforts to formalize them within legal frameworks have accelerated — a divergence between codification and use.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Headline legal expansion overstates real-world IP risk; the meaningful metric is licenses actually issued and volumes actually produced.
insights.locator: As the immediate urgency of the pandemic has faded

themes.theme: IP Uncertainty and R&D Capital Allocation

insights.claim: Even when royalties are paid, the possibility that governments may override patents in future crises raises uncertainty about expected returns on high-risk R&D, and for firms whose products need billions of dollars and more than a decade to develop this shapes where they invest, which technologies they pursue, and whether they enter technology transfer partnerships in emerging markets.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The transmission channel from IP policy to capital allocation: expect firms to under-invest in tech transfer precisely in jurisdictions that codify CL.
insights.locator: Difficulty in CL Implementation

insights.claim: For complex therapies such as biologics and mRNA vaccines, patents are only part of what is needed because production requires specialized know-how and manufacturing expertise that compulsory licensing cannot provide, making CL structurally less effective the more advanced the medicine.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Portfolio implication: biologics and mRNA franchises are far more CL-resistant than small molecules, so the mix of a pharma's pipeline determines its real IP-override exposure.
insights.locator: Moreover, for complex therapies such as biologics

insights.claim: Mexico strengthened compulsory licensing provisions in its Federal Law for Protection of Industrial Property in 2020 but has yet to issue a single license, deterred by limited domestic production capacity, ties to multinational firms and USMCA commitments — while targeting roughly $2 billion annually in pharmaceutical and biotech R&D by 2030.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A clean case that trade commitments plus FDI ambition neutralize CL statutes in practice — a template for reading other emerging-market IP reforms.
insights.locator: Mexico, for example, despite reforming

insights.claim: In May 2025 the European Union reached a political agreement to establish a bloc-wide compulsory licensing regime for defined cross-border emergencies, characterized here as intended to demonstrate preparedness rather than to fill an operational gap, with similar discussions underway in Turkey, Latin America and Southeast Asia.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: EU-level CL machinery is a new standing legal overhang on pharma IP inside a developed market — monitor implementing regulation and any first invocation.
insights.quote: a move intended to demonstrate preparedness rather than to address an operational gap

insights.claim: South Africa has extended compulsory licensing principles into the copyright domain, now being tested in a 2025 tribunal case, showing the mechanism diffusing beyond pharmaceuticals into other IP-dependent sectors.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Spillover risk: if CL logic migrates to copyright, media, software and content-licensing businesses inherit an IP-override tail risk they have not priced.
insights.locator: South Africa’s recent extension of compulsory licensing principles

insights.claim: Codifying compulsory licensing functions as a symbol of health equity, and the political incentive for a government to blame an often-foreign company for its own delivery failures — rather than build capacity or credit domestic licensees — is expected to persist after crises end.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Blame-shifting is a durable political payoff, meaning CL rhetoric recurs independently of whether it delivers medicine — a persistent headline-risk generator for global pharma.
insights.locator: Codifying a CL is seen as a symbol of health equity

insights.claim: Without sustained investment in manufacturing capacity, incentives for technology transfer and mechanisms protecting proprietary know-how while enabling access, compulsory licensing remains a legal gesture rather than a practical tool.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The bottom line for positioning: fund and follow biomanufacturing capacity build-out, because that — not IP law — is what changes access outcomes.
insights.quote: compulsory licensing risks becoming a legal gesture than a practical tool
insights.locator: While compulsory licensing has gained new political appeal
